question: On the planning single-engine piston aeroplane, how is propeller rpm controlled?

options.text: Directly by the throttle lever, as the propeller has a fixed pitch
Automatically by the mixture control as the aeroplane climbs
By the manifold pressure gauge acting on a governor valve in the intake
By the pilot with the rpm (pitch) lever of a constant speed propeller

explanation: The aeroplane has a constant speed propeller; the pilot sets the rpm with the rpm or pitch lever and the governor holds it.

question: In what units is the manifold pressure of the planning piston aeroplane shown?
explanation: Manifold pressure is measured in inches of mercury, for example "25.0 inHg".

question: What does a higher manifold pressure mean for the piston engine?

options.text: The propeller rpm has been reduced
More fuel/air mixture is being burnt
The mixture has been leaned further
The engine is at full throttle height

explanation: Total fuel/air mixture entering the engine is varied with manifold pressure: the higher the pressure, the more mixture is burnt and the more power is produced.

question: What is "full throttle height"?

options.text: The height above the airfield at which climb power is reduced to cruise power
The altitude at which the mixture must first be leaned for the best economy
The highest altitude at which the propeller can still reach maximum rpm
The altitude above which the selected manifold pressure can no longer be maintained

explanation: As the aircraft climbs the throttle is advanced to hold manifold pressure. Eventually the throttle is fully forward and manifold pressure starts to fall: that altitude is full throttle height.

question: What happens to manifold pressure in a climb above full throttle height?

options.text: It returns to the take-off value automatically
It increases, as the air becomes thinner
It decreases, with the throttle fully open
It stays constant, held by the governor

explanation: Above full throttle height the throttle is already fully forward, so manifold pressure falls as the aircraft climbs.

question: What is the maximum take-off mass of the planning single-engine piston aeroplane?
explanation: The planning single-engine aeroplane has a maximum take-off mass and a maximum landing mass of 3650 lb.

question: What is the maximum fuel load of the planning single-engine piston aeroplane?
explanation: Its maximum fuel load is 74 US gallons, which at 6 lb/US gal is 444 lb.

question: Unless told otherwise, what fuel density is used for the planning piston aeroplanes?
explanation: A density of 6 lb per US gallon is used unless the question states another value.

question: A full fuel load of 74 US gal at 6 lb/US gal weighs how much?
The single-engine aeroplane's maximum take-off mass is 3650 lb. With full fuel of 444 lb, what is the most the aeroplane can weigh without fuel?
explanation: 3650 − 444 = 3206 lb. Any more and full fuel would take it over the maximum take-off mass.

question: A cruise fuel flow is 66 lb/h. At 6 lb/US gal, what is it in US gallons per hour?
explanation: 66 ÷ 6 = 11 US gallons per hour.

question: In what configuration do the planning piston aeroplane's climb, cruise and descent data assume the undercarriage to be?
explanation: The tables assume the undercarriage is down for take-off and landing and up for climb, cruise and descent. Abnormal cases are not considered.

question: What does the single-engine climb graph give?

options.text: Time, fuel and air distance to climb from mean sea level to a pressure altitude
Time, fuel and ground distance to climb from the airfield to a flight level
Rate of climb and climb gradient for each aeroplane mass at each pressure altitude and temperature
The best climb speed and the full throttle height for each temperature

explanation: The graph gives time, fuel and distance (in NAM) to climb from MSL to any pressure altitude at a given OAT and mass.

question: How is the climb from an airfield above sea level worked out from the climb graph?

options.text: Read the figures for the height difference as if starting at sea level
Read the figures for the cruise level and add those for the airfield
Read the figures for the cruise level and subtract those for the airfield
Read the figures for the airfield only and double them for the climb

explanation: The graph starts at MSL. Extract time, fuel and distance for the top of climb, then for the airfield, and subtract the airfield values.

question: From mean sea level, a climb to FL110 takes 15 min, 5.5 US gal and 32 NAM. From MSL to the 4000 ft airfield the graph gives 4 min, 1.5 US gal and 7 NAM. What does the climb from the airfield take?
explanation: Subtract the airfield values from the top of climb values: 15 − 4 = 11 min, 5.5 − 1.5 = 4 US gal, 32 − 7 = 25 NAM.

question: A climb covers 25 NAM in 11 minutes with a 20 kt headwind component. What is the ground distance?
Is the distance read from the single-engine climb graph a ground distance or an air distance?

options.text: An air distance that already allows for wind
An air distance, to be corrected for the wind
A ground distance in still air at ISA only
A ground distance, already allowing for wind

explanation: The climb graph gives NAM. To find the ground distance, apply the wind component with NGM = NAM ± WC/60 × time.

question: Why is the OAT needed at both the airfield and the cruise level when using the climb graph?

options.text: The average of the two OATs gives the climb TAS
The graph is entered with pressure altitude and temperature at each level
The graph uses OAT only to find the full throttle height for the climb power setting
The OATs are needed only to work out the density altitude

explanation: Time, fuel and distance depend on air density, so each level is entered with its pressure altitude and its OAT.

question: What does each single-engine cruise power setting table give?

options.text: The time, fuel and distance to cruise between two given flight levels
Range and endurance in still air for every power setting at one chosen cruising altitude
TAS, IAS and fuel flow for one power setting at each pressure altitude and temperature
Manifold pressure needed to reach a given TAS at each pressure altitude

explanation: Each table is for one manifold pressure and rpm. It gives TAS, IAS and fuel flow by pressure altitude for a standard day, ISA +20°C and ISA −20°C.

question: For which temperature deviations are the single-engine cruise tables printed?

options.text: Standard day only, with a correction factor

explanation: The tables are printed for a standard day, ISA +20°C and ISA −20°C. Other deviations need interpolation.

question: The forecast temperature at the cruise level is ISA +10°C. How are the single-engine cruise tables used?

options.text: Interpolate between the ISA −20°C and ISA +20°C tables
Interpolate between the standard day and ISA +20°C tables
Use the ISA +20°C table, as it is the nearest higher value
Use the standard day table and add 10 kt to the TAS

explanation: Choose the table nearest the forecast deviation; ISA ±10°C lies halfway between two tables, so interpolate between them.

question: In a single-engine cruise table at FL100, the standard day TAS is 157 kt and fuel flow 11.0 GPH; at ISA +20°C they are 156 kt and 10.7 GPH. What are they at ISA +10°C?
explanation: ISA +10°C is halfway, so take the average of each pair: 156.5 kt and 10.85 GPH.

question: What do the shaded manifold pressure values in a single-engine cruise table indicate?

options.text: They may be used only with the mixture set to full rich
Above full throttle height, they are about the maximum the engine can give
They are the most economical settings for that altitude and temperature
They are the settings for the take-off and initial climb

explanation: Above full throttle height the stated manifold pressure cannot be produced; the shaded values are approximately the maximum available.

question: At FL80 the OAT is +4°C. What is the ISA deviation?
explanation: ISA at FL80 is 15 − (2 × 8) = −1°C. +4°C is 5°C warmer: ISA +5°C.

question: At FL120 the OAT is −19°C. What is the ISA deviation?
explanation: ISA at FL120 is 15 − 24 = −9°C. −19°C is 10°C colder: ISA −10°C.

question: Which interpolation is normally required when using the single-engine cruise tables?

options.text: Between rpm settings, as each table has several rpm columns
Between pressure altitudes, and between temperature tables for ±10°C
Between masses, as each cruise table is printed for one aeroplane mass only
Between wind components, as each table has a headwind column

explanation: The tables are printed at intervals of pressure altitude and for three temperatures, so interpolation is needed between altitudes and, for ISA ±10°C, between tables.

question: What does the single-engine range profile give?

options.text: Maximum ground range, in NGM, at the best range speed for each wind component
Maximum range in still air for each aeroplane mass at the best economy setting
Maximum still air range, in NAM, for four power settings at a chosen pressure altitude
Time, fuel and distance to climb to the best range altitude for each power setting

explanation: The range profile gives an estimate of maximum still air range (NAM) for each of four power settings at a selected pressure altitude.

question: Which fuel allowances are included in the single-engine range profile?

options.text: Climb, cruise, descent and a 5% contingency of the trip fuel for the flight
Taxi and run-up, climb, cruise and a 45-minute reserve at economy cruise power
Taxi, climb and cruise, with a 30-minute reserve at holding speed at 1500 ft above destination
Climb and cruise only, with no allowance for taxi or for any reserve at all

explanation: The range allows for taxi and run-up, climb, cruise, and a reserve of 45 minutes at economy cruise power.

question: The single-engine range profile gives a range in NAM. What must be done before using it for a route?

options.text: Convert it to NGM using the wind component and the TAS shown
Correct it for the aeroplane's mass using the mass correction table
Add the taxi and climb distance, which are not included in it
Reduce it by 45 minutes of flying, as the reserve is not included

explanation: Range is affected by wind. The graph shows TAS at 4000, 8000 and 12 000 ft, which is used with the wind component to convert NAM into NGM.

question: The single-engine range profile gives 820 NAM with a TAS of 160 kt. The wind component is 30 kt head. What is the ground range?
The single-engine range profile gives 760 NAM with a TAS of 165 kt. The wind component is 25 kt tail. What is the ground range?
At which altitudes does the single-engine range profile quote TAS on each power curve?

options.text: Only at the best range altitude

explanation: TAS is quoted at 4000, 8000 and 12 000 ft; interpolation may be needed for other altitudes.

question: Why is the endurance from the single-engine endurance profile called a "safe endurance"?

options.text: It assumes a 30-minute reserve at 1500 ft
It is reduced by 10% for fuel gauge error
It assumes the mixture is set to full rich

explanation: The endurance includes a 45-minute reserve, so the figure is a safe endurance.

question: How does a headwind affect the endurance read from the single-engine endurance profile?
explanation: Endurance is time airborne, which depends on fuel flow through the air. Wind changes distance over the ground, not the endurance.

question: Is the single-engine endurance figure necessarily the time to achieve maximum range?

options.text: Yes, but only at the full throttle setting
Yes, they are always flown at the same speed
No, endurance is always the longer time
No, endurance and range are different optima

explanation: Endurance is how long the aeroplane can stay airborne; it is not necessarily the time to fly the maximum range, which uses a different speed.

question: An endurance profile gives 5.4 hours. What is that in hours and minutes?
explanation: 0.4 h is 0.4 × 60 = 24 minutes, so 5.4 h is 5 h 24 min.

question: An endurance profile gives 6.35 hours. What is that in hours and minutes?
explanation: 0.35 h is 21 minutes, so 6.35 h is 6 h 21 min.

question: On a single-engine fuel log, a leg is 82 NGM at a ground speed of 168 kt with a fuel flow of 11.9 GPH. What are the leg time and fuel?
On a single-engine fuel log, a leg is 150 NGM at a ground speed of 166 kt with a fuel flow of 11.0 GPH. What are the leg time and fuel?
On a fuel log in light and variable winds, the climb covers 18 NAM. The first leg from the departure airfield to point B is 100 NM. How long is the leg from top of climb to B?
explanation: With no wind NAM equals NGM, so the climb uses 18 NM of the leg, leaving 100 − 18 = 82 NM from top of climb to B.

question: On a single-engine fuel log, why is the climb distance subtracted from the first leg distance?

options.text: The cruise starts only at the top of climb, part way along the first leg
The climb is flown at a lower TAS, so it covers no ground distance
The first leg distance on the chart already includes the descent distance
The climb fuel is included in the taxi allowance and is not logged

explanation: The first leg starts at the airfield, but cruise data apply only from top of climb. The cruise part of the leg is the leg distance less the climb ground distance.

question: A single-engine aeroplane cruises 200 NGM at a ground speed of 150 kt with a fuel flow of 10.5 GPH. How much fuel is used?
